questions.q: In the ring collective time formula T_comm ≈ 2 × (N-1)/N × (S/β), what happens to the per-GPU communication time as N (the number of GPUs) grows very large?
options: It grows proportionally with N
It shrinks to zero
It stays roughly constant, since (N-1)/N approaches 1
It doubles every time N doubles
questions.explain: As N grows large, (N-1)/N approaches 1, so the per-GPU communication time stays roughly flat regardless of cluster size — it doesn't shrink just because more GPUs were added.

questions.q: Why does the compute-to-communication ratio get worse, not better, as a training cluster scales out to more GPUs?
options: Because communication time increases with more GPUs while compute time stays flat
Because per-GPU compute time shrinks (each GPU does less work) while per-GPU communication time stays roughly flat
Because more GPUs always means slower networks
Because adding GPUs increases the model's parameter count
questions.explain: Per-GPU compute time decreases as work is split across more GPUs, but per-GPU communication time stays roughly constant per the ring collective formula — so communication becomes a larger fraction of each step as the cluster grows.

questions.q: What is 'compute-communication overlap,' and why does it help?
options: Running two separate training jobs on the same GPUs at once
Starting the communication (e.g., AllReduce) for one part of the model while compute continues on another part, instead of doing them strictly in sequence
Doubling the InfiniBand bandwidth
Running the backward pass twice for redundancy
questions.explain: Overlap means NCCL can begin reducing gradients for an already-computed layer while the backward pass continues computing gradients for other layers — hiding communication latency behind ongoing compute rather than waiting for it serially.

questions.q: Roughly how much data does this lesson estimate moves collectively through solara-train's fabric on each training step for Solara-70B?
options: About 2.8 MB
About 28 GB
About 280 GB
About 2.8 TB
questions.explain: With 70 billion parameters and roughly 2 bytes each for both parameters and gradients in BF16 under FSDP's reduce-scatter/all-gather pattern, the collective data movement per step is on the order of 280 GB.

questions.q: Why was network bandwidth a less pressing concern within a single 8-GPU node compared to across 512 GPUs?
options: Because single-node training doesn't use any network at all

Because intra-node GPU-to-GPU communication uses NVLink's much higher bandwidth, while inter-node communication relies on the comparatively lower-bandwidth InfiniBand fabric that the ring formula's flat per-GPU cost applies to at scale
Because a single node has no gradients to synchronize
Because FSDP is not used within a single node
questions.explain: Within a node, NVLink provides very high bandwidth (up to 900 GB/s per GPU), making communication nearly free by comparison. Once training spans many nodes over InfiniBand, the flatter, lower-bandwidth inter-node path becomes the dominant constraint as the formula predicts.
